j.learned_fact: You are a little shorter at the end of the day than in the morning because your back (spine) gets squished during the day.
j.thinking_skill: Comparing two marks and inferring that his body changed
j.notes: The bee and the sports arena are dangling details with no payoff, and 'Milan was very tall that day' is an odd line; the daily height change (about 1 cm) is barely visible on a wall mark, so the setup is stretched though not false. 'Spine' is high for age 4 and no reason is given for the shrinking.

j.learned_fact: Yeast is alive; it eats sugar in the dough and makes bubbles, and the bubbles make the dough rise.
j.thinking_skill: Asking a causal question ('Did it eat something?') and connecting it to the result
j.notes: Bread being made in a music class, the 'tiny horse' simile and the drums are bolted-on prompt elements that make no sense together; the science itself is delivered cleanly.

j.learned_fact: Russia is the biggest country (spanning eleven time zones) and Vatican City is the smallest, small enough to walk across in about twenty minutes; there are about 195 countries.
j.thinking_skill: Recognising he cannot finish the whole list and choosing a smaller set of booths (planning/prioritising)
j.notes: 'A cookie with frost' misuses 'frost' (should be frosting) and the winter-festival cookie is a random insert; 'eleven time zones' is beyond a 5-year-old. The 'visit every booth' vs 'match every country' ending is muddled.

j.learned_fact: Measuring with feet gives different answers for different people, but ruler marks are the same size everywhere so everyone gets the same number.
j.thinking_skill: Explaining why two measurements disagreed and why standard units fix it
j.notes: The ruler demonstration is vague ('Ten ruler marks, then ten more') and 'That is useless' feels like a planted vocabulary word; otherwise a solid grade 2 measurement story.

j.learned_fact: Velcro was invented by a man who found burrs on his dog, looked at them under a microscope and saw tiny hooks catching on loops.
j.thinking_skill: Transferring an observation (burr sticks to fur) into a design idea (a fastener)
j.notes: Owen's 'invention' presses a burr onto adhesive tape, which would stick to anything, so the demonstration does not actually show hook-and-loop; the true Velcro history is then dropped in as a mother's explanation. 'Loyal', 'border', 'attempt' and 'adhesive' read as forced vocabulary ('began to attempt gluing' is clumsy).

j.learned_fact: Venice is built on over a hundred small islands joined by bridges, so there are no cars and everything, even mail and groceries, travels by boat.
j.thinking_skill: Sorting photos into two categories and generating what-if questions about consequences
j.notes: 'Combine the photos into two groups' misuses 'combine' (he is sorting/separating), 'a mammal like a dog' is forced, and 'she would daring enough' is a grammatical error; the pasta-making is set up and abandoned.

j.learned_fact: Sound travels about four times faster through water than air and about fifteen times faster through steel, so a vibration through metal arrives before the same sound through air.
j.thinking_skill: Analogical reasoning: mapping sound conduction in steel onto legato phrasing on the drum
j.notes: The setup is implausible (a teacher texts someone to summon a train whistle; a parking-lot footbridge railing would not carry a train's rumble ahead of the air sound) and the physics-to-phrasing analogy is strained. 'Persevere', 'voluntary' and 'concept' are inserted rather than natural ('some voluntary practice at home').

j.learned_fact: FALSE as stated: blowing across a bottle with more water gives a HIGHER note (shorter air column), not a lower one. The story says the fuller bottle blew lower, then has Anthony call it 'backwards' while describing the same direction as tapping. Only the vague idea that tapping and blowing involve different vibrating things is true.
j.thinking_skill: Hypothesising that two different mechanisms produce the two patterns
j.notes: The central observation is wrong and self-contradictory ('That's backwards... more water makes a lower note too'), so the reasoning that follows is incoherent; 'half of the revolution in his understanding' misuses 'revolution' and 'coherent pattern' is forced.

j.learned_fact: The boiling point of water depends on pressure: at high altitude (low pressure) it boils below 100 C so food cooks slowly, and in a sealed pressure cooker it reaches about 120 C so food cooks faster.
j.thinking_skill: Forming a hypothesis from reading and testing it with a controlled comparison (sealed pot vs open pot)
j.notes: The experiment is physically implausible: she reads a kitchen thermometer inside a sealed pressure cooker, and water 'began to boil almost immediately'. The 'why' (vapour pressure must match surrounding pressure) is never given. 'Pendulum' and 'negligible' are correct but noticeably planted.

j.learned_fact: If a website can email you your actual password, it is storing it in readable form, which is dangerous if the site is breached; a secure site can only send a reset link because it does not keep your password.
j.thinking_skill: Inferring hidden system design from observable behaviour via a comparison test
j.notes: The story stops short of the concept it is circling (hashing), so the reader learns the symptom but not the mechanism; 'cordial message' and 'improvise solutions' are inserted vocabulary. Very dialogue-heavy with little scene.

j.learned_fact: Without any greenhouse effect Earth's average temperature would be about minus 18 C; the climate problem is not the effect's existence but its intensification, with CO2 rising from about 300 to 420 parts per million in a century.
j.thinking_skill: Identifying the real point of disagreement (existence vs magnitude) and recognising a strawman argument
j.notes: It is odd that Keisha, after three weeks of preparation, only discovers on debate day that the greenhouse effect is natural, and the parting line 'you could still win this' comes after the debate is over. Otherwise a genuinely well-built argument story.

j.learned_fact: The true lesson is that each flip is independent, the gambler's fallacy is wrong, and a run of five or more in 100 flips is expected. But the numbers given are FALSE: 73, 68 and 81 heads in 100 fair flips are essentially impossible (81 heads is a roughly 10-in-a-billion event), so with those results the code really would be broken, and the stated average 'around fifty-eight' of 73,68,81,55,42,69,59 is actually about 64.
j.thinking_skill: Reconciling independence of trials with the inevitability of streaks (probabilistic reasoning)
j.notes: A probability story whose sample numbers contradict its own lesson, plus a wrong average; 'his rapport with uncertainty' misuses 'rapport' and 'implicate something off' misuses 'implicate' (should be indicate). 'Despondent' is overwrought for the moment.

j.learned_fact: A recommendation algorithm optimised for engagement rewards whatever holds attention (anger, provocation), and a metric you can measure is not the same as what users actually want.
j.thinking_skill: Distinguishing a measurable proxy from the real objective and questioning the optimisation target itself
j.notes: Antoine has only hypothetical users, so the 'engagement' results that drive the epiphany come from data he must have invented, which the story glosses over. 'Tautological' is loose and 'eviscerated any gentle recommendations' is hyperbolic vocabulary planting, though not strictly wrong.

j.learned_fact: The World Wide Web was given away free: released in 1991 and put in the public domain in 1993, which is why anyone can learn from and build on it. (The story states this only vaguely as 'someone convinced their employer to give the whole thing away.') Also: read error messages as diagnostic codes.
j.thinking_skill: Counterfactual reasoning about how open access shaped his own learning
j.notes: Internal contradictions: the grandfather 'sat on that knowledge for three decades' yet learned in his sixties from YouTube; the code 'kept spitting back errors' and has mismatched brackets, yet is 'syntactically valid' so 'the computer isn't throwing a fit'. 'Valorized owning' and 'felt equivocal' are strained, and the web-history fact is too garbled to be securely learned.
